lessons.title: Lesson 1: Planning your family's week
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to turn a messy week into a clear schedule.
This lesson builds toward: Given a busy week of shifts, school and appointments, you will use an AI assistant to turn your list into a day-by-day schedule and fix any clashes, using first names or roles only, with you making the final choices.
When work shifts, school, appointments and errands pile up, it is easy to forget something. An AI assistant can sort your list into a day-by-day plan.
Type everything you need to do this week in any order, with times you already know. Use first names or roles ("my oldest", "Grandma") instead of full names. Then ask: "Put this into a day-by-day schedule. Show what clashes."
Look for clashes, where two things happen at the same time. Ask the AI for ideas, like a carpool or moving an errand, but you make the final choice.
Step by step:
- List everything for the week, in any order, with known times.
- Ask the AI to sort it into a day-by-day schedule and show clashes.
- Ask for ideas to fix each clash.
- Copy the final plan to your phone calendar or a paper on the fridge.
Words to know:
- Schedule: a plan that shows what happens on each day and at what time.
- Clash: when two things are planned for the same time.
Try it now: List everything your household has to do this week. Ask an AI assistant to turn it into a day-by-day schedule and point out any clashes.
You can now turn a busy week into a clear schedule and spot clashes early.

check.q: What should you type first when planning your week with AI?
options: Everything you need to do, with known times
Your family's full names and birthdays
check.why: The AI needs your whole list and known times to sort it into a schedule.

check.q: The AI suggests skipping your child's doctor visit to fix a clash. What do you do?
options: Ask for other ideas, like a carpool, and choose yourself
check.why: The AI gives ideas, but you make the final choice for your family.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Making a meal plan on a budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a week of meals and a shopping list that fits your budget.
This lesson builds toward: Given your household size, budget and the food you have, you will create a five-dinner meal plan and a shopping list with an AI assistant, checking the cost against your store's real prices.
An AI assistant can plan meals around what you already have, what your family likes, and how much you can spend.
Tell it: how many people, your budget, foods your family likes or cannot eat, what is in your kitchen, and how much time you have to cook. Ask for a shopping list grouped by store section.
AI does not know today's prices at your store, so treat its cost guesses as rough. Check the store's weekly ad or app. For health needs like diabetes or allergies, follow your doctor's or dietitian's advice.
Step by step:
- Check what food you already have.
- Tell the AI the number of people, budget, likes, allergies and cooking time.
- Ask for five dinners and a shopping list grouped by store section.
- Compare with your store's real prices and adjust.
Words to know:
- Budget: the amount of money you plan to spend.
- Staples: basic foods you use often, like rice, beans, flour and oil.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for five dinners for your household using foods you already have plus a budget you choose, with a shopping list grouped by store section.
You can now make a budget meal plan and shopping list with AI, and check it against real prices.

check.q: Why group a shopping list by store section?
check.why: Grouping by section, like produce or dairy, saves time in the store.

check.q: You have rice, beans and eggs at home. What do you tell the AI?
options: The foods you already have, so it plans around them
check.why: Planning around food you have saves money and waste.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding local help when money is tight
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a local resource for a real need and check it with an official source.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real need such as food, rent or utilities, you will find one local program through 211 and confirm it with an official source, writing down its official phone number before you go.
Many families need help sometimes: with food, rent, utility bills, child care or a job. Asking for help is part of taking care of your family.
211 is a confidential line that connects people to local help with housing, food, transportation, health care and more. You can dial 211, and many areas also offer text or web chat. Your library and local community center also keep lists of local help.
An AI assistant can help you understand what kinds of help exist and what questions to ask. But it may list places that closed or programs that changed. Always confirm with 211, the program's official website, or a phone call.
Step by step:
- Name the need: food, rent, utilities, child care or jobs.
- Ask an AI what kinds of programs usually help and what to ask them.
- Dial 211 or visit 211.org to find real local programs.
- Call or check the program's official website before you go.
Words to know:
- Resource: a place, program or person that can help with a need.
- Confidential: kept private; not shared without your permission.
Official sources:
- 211.org: About 211
Try it now: Pick one need your family or a neighbor has. Ask an AI what kinds of programs help with it. Then find one real local program through 211.org or by dialing 211, and write down its official phone number.
You can now find a local resource for a real need and confirm it with an official source.

check.q: Besides dialing 211, how else can you often reach it?
check.why: Many areas offer 211 by text or web chat, and online at 211.org.

check.q: A neighbor needs help paying the electric bill. What is a good first step with AI?
options: Ask the AI to pay the bill
Ask what kinds of programs help and what to ask them
Wait until the power is cut off
check.why: AI can explain kinds of help and questions to ask; then you find real programs through 211.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making a meeting agenda
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to write a clear one-page meeting agenda.
This lesson builds toward: For a group you belong to, you will write a one-page meeting agenda with an AI assistant, with topics in order, times, the most important topic early, and time for questions.
Community groups get more done when meetings have a plan. An agenda is a short list of what the meeting will cover, in order, with how much time for each part.
Tell the AI the group, the goal, how long the meeting is, and the topics. For example: "Make a one-hour agenda for our tenants' group. Topics: broken laundry machines, a summer cookout, and choosing a new secretary. Leave time for questions."
Read it with your group's needs in mind. Move topics around, add a welcome, and make sure the most important topic is not squeezed at the end.
Step by step:
- Write down the group, goal, length and topics.
- Ask the AI for a one-page agenda with times for each topic.
- Put the most important topic early.
- Add a welcome and time for questions, then share it before the meeting.
Words to know:
- Agenda: a list of topics for a meeting, in order, with times.
- Secretary: the person in a group who takes notes and keeps records.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to write a one-hour agenda for a real group you belong to, with three topics and time for questions.
You can now make a clear meeting agenda with an AI assistant.

check.q: What four things should an agenda prompt tell the AI?
options: The group, goal, length and topics
check.why: With the group, goal, length and topics, the AI can make a useful agenda.

check.q: The AI put choosing a new secretary last, with 5 minutes. It is your main topic. What do you do?
options: Move it earlier and give it more time
check.why: The most important topic should come early so it is not squeezed at the end.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Writing clear group messages and notes
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a meeting reminder and turn rough notes into a short summary.
This lesson builds toward: Before and after a group meeting, you will write a reminder and turn rough notes into a summary with action items, with no private details, and checked with someone who was there.
A good reminder says what, when, where, and what to bring, in a few short lines. Ask the AI for one in a friendly tone, and for a second version in another language if your group needs it.
After the meeting, AI can turn rough notes into a clean summary: what was decided, who will do what, and by when. Leave out private details, like someone's health or money troubles.
Before sending, check names, dates and decisions with someone who was there. A summary must match what really happened.
Step by step:
- Ask for a friendly reminder with what, when, where and what to bring.
- Ask for a second-language version if needed.
- After the meeting, paste your rough notes without private details.
- Ask for a summary: decisions, who does what, and by when.
- Check it with someone who was there, then send.
Words to know:
- Summary: a short version that keeps only the main points.
- Action item: a task someone agreed to do after a meeting.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a three-line reminder for the meeting from Lesson 4. Then write five rough practice notes and ask it to turn them into a summary with action items.
You can now write clear meeting reminders and turn notes into a summary with action items.

check.q: What does a meeting summary list?
options: Decisions, who does what, and by when
check.why: A summary shows what was decided and who will do what by when.

check.q: Your rough notes say a member is behind on rent. What do you do before pasting them into AI?
options: Leave it in; it is useful
Send the notes to the whole street
check.why: Private details about someone's money or health stay out of AI prompts and summaries.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making a community resource list
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a one-page list of local help that you checked yourself.
This lesson builds toward: For three needs in your community, you will create a one-page resource list with official numbers and hours you checked yourself, dated with when you checked it.
A resource list helps neighbors find help fast. Keep it to one page: the type of help, the program name, the official phone number or website, and the hours.
Use AI to set up the layout and explain each program in one plain sentence. Get the real names, numbers and hours from 211, the program's official website, or a phone call, not from the AI.
Put the date at the bottom ("Checked on ..."). Programs change, so check the list again every few months.
Step by step:
- Choose three needs your community has.
- Find one real program for each through 211 or official websites.
- Ask the AI for a simple one-page layout and a plain one-line description of each.
- Fill in the official numbers and hours yourself.
- Add the date you checked it.
Words to know:
- Layout: how words and boxes are arranged on a page.
Official sources:
- 211.org: find your local 211
Try it now: Final task: organize a small meeting for your group with an AI-written agenda and a reminder message, and make a one-page list of three local help resources you checked yourself.
You can now organize a community meeting and share a checked list of local help.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Agenda No agenda, or topics without order or times. One page with topics in order, times, and time for questions. The most important topic is early, and there is a welcome. Reminder message Missing what, when or where. A short, friendly reminder with what, when, where and what to bring. Also has a second-language version the group needs. Resources checked Programs or numbers came from the AI and were not checked. Three real local programs, each confirmed through 211, an official site or a call. Can say how each one was checked. Resource list layout Missing phone numbers, hours or a date. One page with type of help, program, official number or site, hours, and a "Checked on" date. Each program has a plain one-line description. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What four things go on each line of a resource list?
options: Type of help, program name, official phone or website, and hours
check.why: These four things let neighbors find and reach the help fast.

check.q: The AI fills in a phone number for a food pantry. What do you do?
options: Remove the pantry from the list
Replace it with the number from 211 or the official site
check.why: Real numbers and hours come from 211 or official sources, not from the AI.
